system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

Division of Vascular and Endovascular Surgery
Angioplasty/Stent Discharge Instructions

Medications:
Take Aspirin 325mg (enteric coated) once daily 
If instructed, take Plavix (Clopidogrel) 75mg once daily
Continue all other medications you were taking before surgery, 
unless otherwise directed
You make take Tylenol or prescribed pain medications for any 
post procedure pain or discomfort

What to expect when you go home:
It is normal to have slight swelling of the legs:
Elevate your leg above the level of your heart (use ___ 
pillows or a recliner) every ___ hours throughout the day and at 
night
Avoid prolonged periods of standing or sitting without your 
legs elevated
It is normal to feel tired and have a decreased appetite, your 
appetite will return with time 
Drink plenty of fluids and eat small frequent meals
It is important to eat nutritious food options (high fiber, 
lean meats, vegetables/fruits, low fat, low cholesterol) to 
maintain your strength and assist in wound healing
To avoid constipation: eat a high fiber diet and use stool 
softener while taking pain medication

What activities you can and cannot do:
When you go home, you may walk and go up and down stairs
You may shower (let the soapy water run over groin incision, 
rinse and pat dry)
Your incision may be left uncovered, unless you have small 
amounts of drainage from the wound, then place a dry dressing or 
band aid over the area that is draining, as needed
No heavy lifting, pushing or pulling (greater than 5 lbs) for 
1 week (to allow groin puncture to heal)
After 1 week, you may resume sexual activity
After 1 week, gradually increase your activities and distance 
walked as you can tolerate
No driving until you are no longer taking pain medications
Call and schedule an appointment to be seen in ___ weeks for 
post procedure check and ultrasound 

What to report to office:
Numbness, coldness or pain in lower extremities 
Temperature greater than 101.5F for 24 hours
New or increased drainage from incision or white, yellow or 
green drainage from incisions
Bleeding from groin puncture site

SUDDEN, SEVERE BLEEDING OR SWELLING (Groin puncture site)
Lie down, keep leg straight and have someone apply firm 
pressure to area for 10 minutes. If bleeding stops, call 
vascular office ___. If bleeding does not stop, call 
___ for transfer to closest Emergency Room.

___

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I’m Dr. Patel, one of the vascular surgeons. I understand you’ve been having some issues with high blood pressure lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. My numbers have been really high, even with all my meds. My transplant team said something about the kidney artery being narrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. A recent ultrasound—called a renal artery duplex—showed there’s a narrowing in the artery that supplies blood to your transplanted kidney on the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Could that be why my blood pressure’s so hard to control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. When the artery to the transplanted kidney is narrowed, it can cause what we call 'renovascular hypertension.' Fixing the narrowing might help bring your blood pressure down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what do we do next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do a procedure called an angiogram to get a detailed look at the artery. If we confirm the narrowing, we’ll place a small stent to open it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A stent? Like in the heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very similar. It’s a small metal mesh tube that holds the artery open so blood can flow freely to your kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it risky? I mean, I’ve got the transplant and diabetes…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern. Because your kidney function is already borderline, we’ll use a special technique—CO2 gas instead of regular contrast—to reduce any stress on the kidney during the imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better. When would this happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. Tonight, we’ll keep you here for observation, start some IV fluids to protect your kidneys, and run a few blood tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Should I stop any of my usual meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll hold your furosemide and lisinopril tonight. We’ll restart them once we check your kidney function tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs look stable. Creatinine is 1.8, which is within your usual range. We’re cleared to proceed with the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Any last-minute instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just stay on bed rest after the procedure for a few hours. The team will monitor your groin site where the catheter goes in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, great news. We completed the stent placement successfully. The artery is now open, and blood flow looks excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Did you use the CO2 like we talked about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we used CO2 for the initial imaging, and only a minimal amount of contrast when absolutely needed. Your kidney should handle it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any pain meds? My groin feels a bit sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can take the oxycodone-acetaminophen as needed. Just one tablet every four hours if you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? Should I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart your lisinopril and furosemide tomorrow morning after we check your creatinine again. The rest you can continue as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood thinners? I’m on Plavix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Plavix—now called clopidogrel—as part of your discharge meds. It helps keep the stent open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And aspirin too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll take both aspirin and clopidogrel daily. This dual therapy is important for the first few months after stenting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are stable, and your vital signs are good. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That was fast. Any restrictions when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. No heavy lifting—nothing over five pounds—for at least a week. That helps the groin puncture heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off on driving until you’re off the pain medication. Once you’re not taking oxycodone, you can start again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the incision? Can I shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can shower. Let the water run over the area, then pat it dry. No need to cover it unless there’s a little drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for? When should I call?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have fever over 101.5, pain or coldness in your leg, or bleeding from the groin. If there’s sudden swelling or severe bleeding, lie down, keep your leg straight, and have someone press on the area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your transplant team and me in two weeks. We’ll do a follow-up ultrasound to make sure the stent is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better knowing we’re addressing the blood pressure issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up with your diabetes and blood pressure meds, eat well, and take it easy for a few days. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications one more time, then you can head home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. Looking forward to getting back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take care, and we’ll see you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old male with a history of kidney transplant, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for evaluation and treatment of right renal artery stenosis, which was contributing to poorly controlled hypertension. A renal artery duplex ultrasound suggested significant narrowing, prompting an endovascular procedure. The patient underwent a successful renal arteriogram with CO2 contrast followed by placement of a non-drug-eluting stent in the right transplanted renal artery. The procedure was uncomplicated, and postoperative labs showed stable renal function. The patient was monitored for 24 hours, restarted on antihypertensives, and discharged home in stable condition with instructions for activity restrictions, wound care, and dual antiplatelet therapy. Follow-up was arranged with vascular surgery and transplant nephrology in two weeks for clinical assessment and surveillance imaging.
